style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: We're continuing with the content rubric.
Development of ideas. How varied your arguments are, and how logical and full each one is.
Let's start with variety. Say my first argument paragraph is against the cameras.
In my opinion, they should not be allowed, since it will violate the public's right to privacy.
That's true, and of course I'd have to go on and explain it. But right now we're not talking about the explanation. We're talking about variety.
Now, the second paragraph.
In addition, installing face-recognition cameras may give security authorities the personal information of private people without their consent.
Wait. We have a problem here. There's no variety.
One talks about the right to privacy. The other talks about personal information taken without consent. It's the same thing, in other words.
Privacy is general, and the second one is a bit more specific. But it's not a different angle. It's the same narrow point of view.
So let's see how to make it better.
In addition, the cameras may not reduce crime, since criminals won't stop. They'll move their activity to unmonitored areas.
Now this is a varied argument. First I was against the cameras because they harm privacy.
And now I'm against the cameras because they won't help. There won't be less crime. It'll just move. Not in the public space? Fine, let's do it next door.
That's a nice example of arguments from different points of view. It shows high critical thinking.
Of course, all of this is very short. We still need to develop it, add details, and explain it.
So our arguments need to be varied.
And finding varied arguments is one of the things students struggle with most.
Later we have lessons on three ways to find arguments. From the task, who is involved and how it affects them, and points of view.
I won't say more about those names now. But they make finding varied arguments much, much easier.
Now the second part. How logical and full each argument is. The reader has to see how you got from your claim to your result.
In my opinion, they should be allowed, since the cameras will reduce crime. When a person's behaviour is monitored, the chance that he'll behave according to accepted social norms increases.
Therefore, the cameras will cause criminals to avoid committing crimes and will protect the population.
This paragraph is a bit too short. The argument isn't full enough. It's not detailed enough.
So where exactly is the gap?
It talks about social norms, and then suddenly I jump straight to criminals, crimes, and protecting the population.
Why would norms of behaviour explain what a criminal decides? And how exactly does that protect the population? The steps are missing.
The fix is to fill in the missing links, so each step leads to the next.
Now, an argument that's full and detailed.
In my opinion, they should not be allowed, since it will not reduce crime.
When I read only this key sentence, it sounds strange. Really? It sounds logical to me that cameras reduce crime. How can that be? Explain it to me.
So he explains. The cameras won't be installed secretly. The public will know it's being recorded. Okay, true.
Assuming criminals know it too, and they will, they may not stop. A criminal still 'needs his salary'. Stealing is his job.
So he won't steal here. He'll steal there. That doesn't mean he steals less. Crime doesn't shrink... it just moves.
Look at the steps he gave us.
If this, then this, then this. And here we are at the result. Crime won't really go down.
Maybe. It's his opinion. But it's an opinion he explained, step by step.
And notice... the stranger the key sentence sounds at first, the more the reader needs these steps.
So development means two things. Varied reasons, and full explanations. Next criterion: focus and coherence.
Now it's your turn. Workshop 4, the missing link. It's in the card right after this lesson.
Do it before you move on. Each assignment builds on the one before, and by the end of the lessons you'll have written whole essays.
